extracted.intended_audience: classical scholars, textual critics, and advanced students working on Aristotle (esp. the Poetics) and manuscript editing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for interpreting and editing Aristotle's Poetics: principles for choosing readings, detecting interpolations, using manuscript and versional evidence, and for what counts as an acceptable interpretation of Aristotle. Emphasises internal consistency with Aristotle's works, manuscript-stemma reasoning, and philological caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate aim of textual criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate aim of textual criticism is to restore the work of an author to the condition in which it left his hands; if that is impossible, an intermediate aim is to restore the text as it existed at some particular epoch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all extant copies descend from a later archetype (later than the author's copy) and that archetype has perished, restore the intermediate stage before attempting anything more original. This frames priorities when perfect recovery is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of internal and external evidence for stemma claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Convincing internal evidence would be defects shared by all MSS traceable to a single exemplar; convincing external evidence would be reliable testimony that a particular MS was the first brought to a region or that other MSS derive from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require either internal signs (e.g., identical lacunae, corruptions that point to a single ancestor) or strong external testimony before asserting that all MSS are copies of a single source (A). Be explicit about what evidence would convince you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume easier readings are preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a manuscript offers an easier or smoother text than another, one must not automatically prefer it as original; such smoothing can indicate deliberate emendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the 'easier' reading could be a later deliberate correction. Use other witnesses (e.g., Arabic version) and internal style evidence to judge. Beware that apparent simplicity may mask interpolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for readings corroborated by independent witnesses and versional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Readings supported by independent MSS or by an independent version (e.g., Arabic) should be given weight, especially where the primary MS (A) is corrupt or unintelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Arabic and other independent witnesses to guard against corruptions in A; but note that Arabic can also conspire with other MSS in joint amateur emendations—examine patterns rather than trusting single agreements blindly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting interpolations by linguistic and stylistic anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, constructions, or forms that are non-Greek, un-Aristotelian, or otherwise anomalous (e.g., improbable word-forms, prepositional anastrophe, non-Greek coinages) are signs of interpolation or later alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag readings like συνθήσεις or odd preposition choices as probable interpolations. Corroborate by checking Aristotle's idiom elsewhere and related works; check for Greekness and conformity to author's fixed formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for every syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: No interpretation is satisfactory which fails to account for every syllable of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable reading/interpretation should make sense of the whole surface text; do not ignore or leave unexplained words, particles, or inflections. When emendation is proposed, justify how it explains problematic syllables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite chapter and verse for certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: No interpretation is certain for which chapter and verse cannot be cited from Aristotle’s works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base interpretative claims on citations or parallels from Aristotle's corpus (chapter and verse) wherever possible. Use his other works to test proposed senses and to supply authoritative context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject attributions that are meaningless or contrary to common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: No interpretation is tolerable which ascribes to Aristotle propositions which are unmeaning or which conflict with common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reading forces the ascription of absurd, unintelligible, or implausible doctrines to Aristotle, prefer alternative readings even if they require emendation. The author is unlikely to violate his own rules or produce nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret passages in light of the author's wider works and doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Key to interpretation is the author's usage elsewhere; properties of technical terms (e.g., μέτρον) and Aristotle's doctrines must inform readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare questionable words/phrases with occurrences in the Metaphysics, Physics, Rhetoric, Ethics, etc., to decide between senses (e.g., μέτρον = metre, measure, extent). Use Aristotle's idiom to choose among ambiguous meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect internal structural dependencies in the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections of the Poetics are interdependent (e.g., §4 is not intelligible without §§6 and 26); understanding earlier parts often requires acquaintance with later parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before construing a passage, check related sections for preparatory arguments or anticipations. Do not isolate sentences from the treatise's internal argument structure when interpreting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider manuscript provenance and historical transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical circumstances (ownership, dating, events such as the fall of Constantinople) affect probabilities about how MSS relate and where readings may have arisen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provenance, dated copies, and historical events to assess whether MSS could share a common ancestor or were dispersed at given times. Weigh likelihoods (e.g., dispersal as loot after 1453) when reconstructing stemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and philosophical sense to resolve textual difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where readings conflict, appeal to philosophical/technical sense (e.g., genus/species usage, Aristotle's concepts) and analogy with other passages to choose the most coherent reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conceptual distinctions (genus vs. species; measure vs. metre) and check parallels in other works to decide between alternative restitutions. Prefer readings that yield coherent philosophical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about conjectural emendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjectural emendations should be avoided unless necessary and should be justified; some MS readings (even awkward ones) may preserve genuine tradition that cannot be restored by conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce conjectures lightly; when proposing emendations, show why existing readings are untenable and why the conjecture is preferable, considering support from versions, parallel passages, and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and interrogate manuscript 'conspiracies'
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes two or more witnesses (including versional witnesses) may jointly reflect the same later alteration or amateur emendation rather than the original text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple witnesses agree, investigate whether agreement stems from shared corruption or deliberate change. Look for internal inconsistencies or signs of tampering (e.g., non-Greek forms) before treating agreement as proof of originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain apparent contradictions by semantic ranges and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent textual contradictions (e.g., statements about epopoiia and Tragedy) should be reconciled by examining semantic ranges of key words and how ordinary usage might differ from technical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., distinguish popular vs technical meanings of epopoiia (hexametric fabrication vs romance) and show how confusion or metaphorical usage could produce the surface text. Use lexical and contextual analysis to reconcile difficulties.
